notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0108f.stoa004.opp-l: The 'about' line is mistaken: the consuls Basiliscus and Herminericus date this to 465, and the synod is Pope Hilarus's Roman synod of that year, not Symmachus's of 499. Line 1 is garbled: the sees and provinces seem displaced (Maximus of Turin belonged to the province of Milan, Ingenuus of Embrun and Saturninus of Avignon to Gaul), and a name is missing before 'Mediolanensi provinciae'. 'SS.' is taken as 'suprascriptae' (aforesaid); this is uncertain. Several sees are unidentified or doubtful and have been kept close to the Latin: Abitia, Faberia, Casitaum, Pansala, Veccona, Trifena, Anteatum. 'Uranus' has no see. 'Pallallius' and 'Soter' (printed 'Solere') are probable readings. 'Nundinatius' is read as Nundinarius. In 47, 'divinationes' is read as 'ordinationes'. 'Matutinus iterare' is read as 'maturius iteramus'. 'Properum' is read as 'praeproperum'. 'Delectu' in 44 may be 'defectu' (failure), not 'through [ill] choice'.

48: 'aut mulierem duxisse' is terse; presumably a woman forbidden by the canons (e.g. a widow). 51: 'retundi' read for 'retun ii', 'veniam' for 'ventam'; several town names uncertain (Ascantenses, Varegenses kept as given; Tritienses, Levienses, Virovescenses taken as Tricio, Libia, Briviesca). 57: 'Basilico' read as Basiliscus. 59: 'perpeteras' read for 'pe teras'. 61: 'Aufiniensis' (Aufinum) assumed for 'Auliniensis'; 'vasa'/'ministeria' taken as sacred vessels.

Several see names are uncertain identifications: 'Anteatino' (Felix of Anteate?), 'Mibanati' (taken as Mevania, reading Innocentio for 'lonocentio'), 'Subaugustano', 'Lorensi' (Lorium?), 'Aquævivensi'. Line 92: the see of Victor is lost in the edition. Under 'Et presbyteris:' the list of presbyters is not given in this text. In 109 the sentence beginning 'Sciens quod se decipiat' is grammatically defective; '[Let him know]' supplies the sense. In 112 'lucris' is read as 'pueris'. The heading says A.D. 487 but the letter's dating gives 488; both are reproduced as printed.

In decree II, 'non nocto judicio' is evidently corrupt; read as 'non recto (or sano) judicio', 'not by sound judgement'. In Symmachus' closing speech (ref 121) the text is disturbed: 'patique constituit' is unclear (perhaps 'paterque' or 'pastorque', rendered '[the father] has decreed'), and 'atque omnes, sine personae alicujus distinctione venire praesumpserit' seems to need 'quisquis' for 'omnes'; translated accordingly. Ref 182 is a fragment with the start of the name lost. Several sees are uncertain or unidentified: Blenarus (taken as Blera), Mibanatis (taken as Mevania), Ferentininovi (Ferentinum Novum?), Calenotanus (taken as Cales), Fulgentanus (taken as Fulginiae), Vivonensis (taken as Vibo), Subaugestanus (Subaugusta), and Forbiensis (left unidentified). 'Malensis' as a personal name is odd and may be corrupt. Titles 'Tigridae'/'Trigridae' are treated as one title, Tigrida, and 'Vizantis' as Byzans. 'Crescentiae' (ref 253) is taken as Crescentiana. The heading says 75 bishops and 67 presbyters subscribed, but the lists as printed give fewer names. Line 10: the scan's 'patique' is read as pacique, '(befitting religion) and peace'.

The text of lines 273 ('statutis debere innocentia praesumentis de libertate deliquerit') appears corrupt; the rendering is a conjectural sense. In 268 the final clause of Basilius' decree runs on into 269, where a verb such as 'alienetur' seems to be missing; [be alienated] is supplied. In 270 're pie animarum' is read as 'requie animarum' (repose of souls), and 'in altitudine transferatur' as 'in alterum/aliorsum transferatur' (transferred elsewhere). In 274 'existimatione' is taken as 'aestimatione'. 'Bledanae Ecclesiae' (Maximus' see) is unidentified with certainty. The heading dates the synod to 503, though Avienus junior's consulship is 502.

Line 277: 'effectetur' is evidently corrupt; context requires 'be deprived of' (all force), translated accordingly. Lines 282-342: many sees are uncertain or corrupt in the scan; tentative identifications include Vetellensis (Vercellae?), Taurinatis (Taurinum or Taurianum?), Ignatinus (Egnatia?), Vessanensis, Huslicus Bursentinus (read as Rusticus of Buxentum), Dunensis, Coaniliensis, Tullentinus, Carmejanen., Samninus, Blestinen., Mesenatis, Pellensis, Syranus; Areston Ostiensis duplicates the see of Ostia, and Felix of Nepet appears twice. Line 343: the consular date names Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus (one consul, cos. 502), not two men as the punctuation suggests; the passage reporting Symmachus' reply through his bishops ('mandatis canonibus ... culmen humiliat ...') is corrupt and rendered conjecturally, as are 'Italiae suae dare rectorem agnoscentes', 'clar tatem veterem vobis dat, det Christi dote rectoribus', and 'sub hac intemissione' (read as 'intentione/occasione'). The scriptural references are given as printed (e.g. 'Ezech. IX' for 'Vengeance is mine', which is Rom. 12 / Deut. 32).

Line 346: two bishops named Hilarus appear (352 'Tempsanus', 366 'Tempranen.'), probably the same see duplicated. Several sees are uncertain identifications and are left as the Latin adjective in italics (Agninus, Tempranensis, Pratensis, Direntium Tiberinorum, Augustanus, Lateranensis, Carmeianensis, Tauriganus, Pallensis); others (e.g. Boensis as Bova, Agnatinus as Anagnia, Acanus as Acerenza, Meresape as Messapia, Celeniensis as Celeia) are tentative. Line 385 'Arnantius' read as Amantius. Line 421: 'Venam' read as 'veniam' (pardon); 'cons. SS.' taken as 'consule suprascripto'. Line 423: 'Joannem Egota n' read as John Aegeates; 'mathema' (Greek 'teaching') kept as 'teaching'; 'subsistentia' rendered 'subsistence' (= hypostasis); 'unitas ... nec ... pax' is syntactically awkward and is rendered as two subjects.

The text has several apparent corruptions; renderings follow the evident sense: 'quod ... paterna omisit instructio' seems to lack a word such as 'nihil' ('omitted [nothing]'); 'aut eum deum et hominem ... prodisse' seems to lack a negation ('[to deny] that he came forth'); 'qualiter habet' read as 'qui aliter habet' ('whoever holds otherwise'); 'adjectione plebis aut institutione perfectis' read as 'adjectione plenis aut instructione perfectis'; 'non admittit essentiae singularitatem' read as 'non amittit' ('does not lose'); 'exspectat' read as 'spectat'; 'ingenitate potentinae' read as 'ingenitae potentiae'. The sense of 'ut nec personis divinitatis singularitas generetur' is unclear and is translated literally. The consular dating 'Valerio Victorio' is given as printed: the consuls of 521 were Valerius and Justinian.

Line 425 breaks off mid-sentence ('pro pheta', 'the prophet'); the letter of Hormisdas is fragmentary here and the text jumps to the Roman synod of Gregory II (A.D. 721). The dating formula 'Anno sexto p. c. ejus anno sexto' seems duplicated. Several see names are identified from garbled forms: 'Beliternensi' as Velitrae (Velletri), 'Maturanensi' as Manturanum, 'Falaris/Faiaritanae' as Falerii, 'Polimartii' as Polimartium (Bomarzo), 'Aodrea' read as Andrea, 'Uviliarit/Vuillari' as Wilihari. 'Gregorio Macoseu' (454) is unidentified and probably corrupt. In 456 'catholicam idem' read as 'fidem', 'alterno judici' as 'aeterno', 'Uinc' as 'Hinc'. The response in 458 is syntactically confused in the printed text. In 472 'anlo emissa' read as 'ante emissa' (previously issued). 'Presbytera' (460) may mean a presbyter's wife or a female cleric; the sense is disputed. In 475 a noun such as 'facto' seems missing after 'crudeli'. The signatures speak in the first person ('subscripsi'), so 'I' has been supplied throughout.

The 'about' line suggests the synod of 499, but these subscriptions and the dating (Leo III and Constantine V, fourth indiction, A.D. 721) belong to the Roman synod under Gregory II. Line 511: 'qua Damasi' is read as 'quae/qui Damasi', i.e. San Lorenzo in Damaso. Line 518: 'Dle non. April.' is read as 'Die nonarum Aprilium' (5 April); the edition's 'PC.' is taken as post consulatum.

nodes.text: SECOND COLLECTION OF DECREES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, ADDED TO THE FIRST COLLECTION OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS.
WHOSE DECREES ARE REVIEWED IN THIS COLLECTION.
IN THE CONSULSHIP OF FLAVIUS BASILISCUS AND HERMINERICUS, MEN MOST DISTINGUISHED.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, the venerable man Pope Hilarus sitting in the basilica of Saint Mary, and Maximus of the city of Turin, of the province of the Gauls; Ingenuus of Embrun, of the aforesaid province; of the province of Milan, of the aforesaid province; Saturninus of Avignon, of the aforesaid province;
Tiberius of Cures of the Sabines;

All the presbyters also sitting, and the deacons standing by, Hilarus, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said: Since this religious assembly, gathered by the Holy Spirit, urges that we should hand down with more diligent care whatever is necessary for ecclesiastical discipline: if it pleases [you], brothers, let us so establish, with the Lord's help, to remain for all time, the things that concern the proper course of ordinations, according to the precepts of the divine law and the decrees of the Nicene canons, that it may be lawful for no one, without peril to his own standing, to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see; for the guilt of such transgressions will fall upon us, who administer the office of the chief priest, if we are found idle in the causes of God, since we remember, as we ought to fear, how the Lord threatens the negligence of priests; for he who enjoys the higher honour offends with the greater guilt, and the loftiness of dignities makes the faults of sinners graver. First of all, therefore, care must be taken that no one who has married a wife not a virgin should aspire to the sacred grades, as was prescribed earlier in former acts. Also to be rejected is anyone who has entered into marriage with a second wife, contrary to the apostolic precepts. Also those ignorant of letters, and those who have suffered some loss of limbs, and those who are from among the penitents, are not to dare to aspire to sacred orders. Whoever has been the consecrator of such men shall himself undo his deed, and what he committed unlawfully, or found admitted by his predecessors, he shall condemn, if he wishes to avoid his own peril: for we wish in no case to exercise the severity of punishment. But whoever has offended in the causes of God through obstinacy or through [ill] choice, or has refused himself to abolish what he did wrongly, will find upon himself whatever he did not cut away in another. And so that this may henceforth be kept more firmly, if it pleases [you], all of you lend your own subscriptions to these cases, so that by synodal judgment the way may be closed to unlawful acts.

By all the bishops and presbyters it was acclaimed: Hear, Christ, life to Hilarus! This was said six times. These things we confirm, these things we teach! Said eight times. These things are to be held, these things are to be kept! Said five times. We give thanks for your teaching! Said ten times. We ask that these things be kept for ever! This was said fifteen times. By the lord Peter, we ask that they be kept for ever! This was said eight times. Let this presumption never happen! Said ten times. Whoever violates these things will find [it] upon himself! Said seven times. And when silence had been made, Bishop Hilarus said: Moreover, brothers, as has reached us in a definite report through letters sent from the Spains, new and unheard-of seeds of perversities are springing up in certain places. In short, some think that the episcopate, which is given only for preceding merits, is not a divine gift but an inherited gain, and believe that the priesthood can be bequeathed, like perishable and mortal things, as if by legal or testamentary right. For many priests, when placed at the edge of death, are said to have others substituted in their place by name: so that, namely, a lawful election is not awaited, but the favour of the deceased is held in place of the people's assent. Consider how grave this is: and therefore, if it pleases [you], let us remove this licence too from the churches generally, so that no one may think, what is shameful to say, that what is God's is owed to men in this way. And so that what has been brought to us may come to your knowledge too, let the letters of our Spanish brothers and fellow bishops be read. Paul the notary read aloud.
To the most blessed Pope Hilarus, to be revered by us in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona.

We have learned what care your apostleship bears for the priests of its provinces from the report of our son, the illustrious Vincentius, duke of our province; at whose urging our wish rose with ready devotion to the venture of writing. Therefore, offering in a provincial letter the obedience due to your crown, we ask by these [lines] that, with the condescension by which [you remember] others, you deign to keep our lowliness also in mind in your prayers, father to be revered by us in Christ with most blessed and apostolic reverence; asking this more especially, that you deign, after weighing our statements, to confirm our action, which is brought to your notice both by the wish of almost the whole province and by the example of antiquity. And while he was reading, it was acclaimed by all the bishops and presbyters: Hear, Christ, life to Hilarus! This was said ten times. Let this presumption never happen! This was said six times. The things that are God's cannot be given by man! This was said six times. By the lord Peter, that they be kept for ever! This was said six times. We ask that these things be kept! Bishop Hilarus said: Read. Paul the notary read aloud. The bishop of the city of the Barcelonans, the holy Nundinarius, fulfilled the lot of the human condition; he, leaving to the venerable bishop our brother Irenaeus, whom he himself had earlier established in his own diocese with our consent, what his poverty could possess, chose by the decision of his last will that he should be substituted in his place; and the judgment of the deceased does not waver as to his merit. And while he was reading, Bishop Probus, rising from his seat, said: That was lawful, this was not lawful. God gives successors; by your authority resist this thing through your apostleship. Bishop Hilarus said: Run through what you had begun. Paul the notary read aloud. Since indeed all the clergy and people of that same city, and the best and most numerous of the provincials, hoped that, consent being given by us, the same [Irenaeus] might occupy his place, we, considering the judgment of the deceased, and approving his life, and the nobility and number of those who were asking, and at the same time the advantage of the said Church, thought it best that for so great a priest, who had passed to the divine, a prelate of no less merit should be substituted, especially since it is established that the Church of that town in which he had been ordained before has always been a diocese of the Church of this city. Therefore we humbly beg your apostleship that by your authority you confirm what seems to have been justly done by our lowliness. Some time ago, indeed, we had complained in our letters of the presumption of Bishop Silvanus, and we wonder that we have received no reply from your apostleship; now, putting forward these same things, we ask that you deign to instruct us in apostolic words what is to be observed in these matters: and lest perhaps, through the negligence of the bearer or the difficulty of the long journey, the letters of our lowliness on this business could not reach you, we are also repeating our representation more promptly. And the subscription: May the divine eternity preserve your holy apostleship, praying for us, for ever, for all of us and for His Church, our true lord and apostolic pope. Bishop Hilarus said: Let the other letter be read. Paul the notary read aloud. To the lord most blessed Pope Hilarus, to be revered by us in Christ with apostolic reverence, Ascanius and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona. Even if no necessity of ecclesiastical discipline existed, we ought truly to have sought that privilege of your see by which, the keys of the kingdom having been received, after the resurrection of the Saviour the singular preaching of the most blessed Peter throughout the whole world provided for the illumination of all; whose vicar's primacy, as it is eminent, so it is to be feared and loved by all. Accordingly, adoring first of all God in you, whom you serve without complaint, we have recourse to the faith praised by the apostolic mouth (Rom. 1), seeking answers from that place where nothing is commanded by error, nothing by presumption, but everything by pontifical deliberation. While these things are so, there is nevertheless among us a false brother, about whose presumption, as it was not permitted to keep silent any longer, so the necessity of the coming judgment has commanded us to speak. Silvanus, bishop of Calagurris, situated in the furthest part of our province, by usurping ordinations not due to him, has brought our lowliness to the point that we demand against his most vain superstition the sole remedy of your see. For this man, already seven or eight or more years ago, setting aside the rules of the Fathers and despising your institutions, ordained a bishop when no people asked for one; and when we thought that his over-hasty deed could be healed by brotherly and peaceful admonition, he went on to worse. Finally, against the antiquity of the canons, against the decrees of the synod, inflamed only by the spirit of presumption, he made a presbyter of another brother of ours a bishop in the same place which had been assigned to that [first] man, a presbyter on whom, unwilling and resisting, he had laid hands, and who had already been joined to our company. Hence it came about that our brother, the bishop of the city of Caesaraugusta, reported to us everything about his most wretched rashness; his diligence and solicitude had looked ahead considerably, if it had been of any avail in anything. For he very often forbade all the bishops placed in the vicinity to join themselves to the schismatic; but with damnable obstinacy that man alone did not blush to commit everything that was unlawful, and what we are ashamed to say. Therefore, since these presumptions, which divide unity, which make schism, must be met quickly, we ask your see that we may be instructed by apostolic utterances what you wish to be observed in this matter, so that, the brotherhood being assembled and the decrees of the venerable synod brought into the open, relying on your authority against the spirit of rebellion, we may with God's help understand what ought to be done both about the ordination and about the one ordained. It will surely be your triumph if, in the times of your apostleship, the catholic Church hears what the chair of Saint Peter holds, if the new seeds of tares have been rooted out. And the subscription: May the divine eternity preserve your holy apostleship, praying for us, for ever. By all the bishops and presbyters it was acclaimed: We ask that these things be corrected! This was said six times. We ask that these things be cut away! This was said seven times. We ask that discipline be kept! Said eight times. We ask that antiquity be kept! Said seven times. We ask that discipline (sic) be kept! This was said five times. We ask that the canons be guarded! This was said seven times. We ask that punishment be taken on the presumptuous! This was said seven times. Let the apostolic ordinance be kept unimpaired! This was said eight times. Hear, Christ, life to Hilarus! This was said five times. Worthy pope, worthy teacher! This was said eight times.

Bishop Hilarus said: Having received what has been read out about all [these matters], now, brothers, with God inspiring us, set forth your individual opinions. Maximus, bishop of the church of Turin, said: In keeping all the disciplines that pertain to holy ordinations, I declare the better by the profession of my opinion that nothing of what has been forbidden is ever to be done by me. As to the rest, I judge that whoever has done such things, or has been unwilling to cut them away when detected in the churches, should know that he will have to answer grave charges in the judgement of the apostolic see: in which he will necessarily have to undergo sentence. Ingenuus, bishop of Embrun, said: I too hold the same opinion on all points, by which I bind myself, that nothing of those things which are forbidden may ever be attempted by me, for I know my state and my profession. Concerning the others too I judge that whoever has proved a transgressor of the statutes should know that he is bound in the snares of the ecclesiastical rule and incurs guilt before the apostolic see. Paul, bishop of Aquaviva, said: I too bind myself by a like law, and concerning the others who have been transgressors I judge likewise, that they may not, without danger to themselves, attempt any such thing as ought rightly to be punished. Primus, bishop of the church of Atella, said: I too judge that this is to be observed. Palladius, bishop of the church of Salapia, said: I promise that I will do nothing against ecclesiastical discipline or the statutes of the holy canons. Tiberius, bishop of the church of Sabina, said: I profess that I keep the statutes of the apostolic see in all things, and that if I discover any of the clergy in my church, against the precepts of the holy canons, either to have married [such] a woman or to have two wives, [he is] to be separated from ecclesiastical office. By all the bishops it was said: We all follow the opinions of the brothers, we all confirm [them], and we decree that they are to be observed. Hear, Christ, life to Hilarus! This was said seven times. Let what has been wrongly committed be corrected through you! This was said eight times. What is not lawful, let it not be done! This was said eight times.

Hilarus, bishop of the church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said: Since we decree that the form of the present definition, which is according to the opinion of the statutes of the saints, should come to the knowledge of all the churches, so that no one may, on the plea of his ignorance, be allowed what is not allowed, the diligence of the notaries will see to publishing the acts.
Bishop Hilarus to Ascanius and all the fellow bishops of the province of Tarragona.

After we received the letter of your love, in which you asked that the presumptions of Silvanus, bishop of the church of Calagurris, be checked, and again you seek that the quite unlawful wishes of the people of Barcelona be confirmed, it is established that letters were delivered to us from the notables and landowners of the cities of Tarazona, *Ascantum*, Calagurris, *Varegia*, Tricio, Libia and Briviesca, with the subscriptions of various persons: by which they excused what your complaint had set forth about Silvanus. But your most just reproof was likewise not lacking in just grounds, since it became clear that priests had been ordained in a number of cities without the knowledge of the metropolitan, our brother and fellow bishop Ascanius. Therefore, since we see that whatever has been reported by either side is confused by every kind of perversity, having taken account of the necessity of the times, we have decided on this basis that what was done falls under pardon, on condition that nothing henceforth be attempted against the precepts of the blessed Apostle, nothing against the constitutions of the Nicene canons.

I. This first we wish to be kept according to the rules of those same Fathers: that no bishop be consecrated in any way without the knowledge and consent of brother Ascanius the metropolitan, because the ancient order has held this, and the authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers has defined it; and whoever stretches out hands against it declares himself unworthy of the fellowship of those whose precepts he has resisted.

II. In contempt of them that part too is despised by a proud spirit which provides that no one, having left his own church, presume to pass to another. This Bishop Irenaeus attempts to commit most shamelessly, with [others] conniving and, to cause greater grief, with you asserting it: you who desire to be strengthened by our authority, whom we find especially roused with great indignation over unlawful things. So, your letter having been read in the assembly of the brothers whom the festival of my anniversary had gathered, you will learn from the tenor of the acts, which we have sent at the same time, the sentence delivered on what has been decreed about ordaining bishops according to the statutes of the canons and of my predecessors.

III. Therefore, Bishop Irenaeus being removed from the church of Barcelona and sent back to his own, and the desires being calmed by priestly restraint which, through ignorance of the church's laws, long to obtain what is not lawful, let a bishop be ordained for the people of Barcelona forthwith from their own clergy, such as it befits you above all, brother Ascanius, to choose and is fitting to consecrate. Lest, if something similar should happen, our command check, not without rebuke chiefly to your name, what we have learned was committed to the injury of God, from whom specially comes the grace of priestly dignities; and let not the episcopal honour be thought a hereditary right, which is conferred on us by the sole kindness of our God Christ.

IV. The bishops now ordained, then, who, although they deserved to be removed with their authors since they were promoted without your knowledge, we confirm on this condition: if none of them has been the husband of a widow, and if he came to marriage with one virgin, and [as] a virgin, just as the legal ordinances also command, saying: Let the priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one divorced (Lev. 21; Ezek. 44); in accordance with which the blessed apostle Paul too, the Teacher of the gentiles, did not keep silent in his own instruction about those who wish to become priests, saying (1 Tim. 3): The husband of one wife; by the tenor of which sentence you ought to be so formed that, among the other things to be guarded against, you strive above all to keep these things which you know are commanded before all else.

V. In these matters too care must be taken that there be not two priests in one church, and that no one ignorant of letters, or lacking some part of his limbs, or also any of the penitents, be allowed at all to approach the sacred ministry. And do not think the petitions of the peoples so powerful that, while you wish to comply with them, you abandon the will of our Lord, which forbids us to sin; whose indignation is moved the more gravely by this, because his kindness is offended when unlawful things are done by those who are the interpreters of propitiation.

VI. And so that all things may be corrected according to what we have written, we have sent the present letter by our subdeacon Trajan, who is coming [to you]. But if Bishop Irenaeus, having laid aside the canvassing of his shamelessness, neglects to return to his own church, which will be granted him not by judgement but by kindness, let him know that he is to be removed from the episcopal fellowship. Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Basiliscus and Herminericus, men of clarissimus rank. (A.D. 465.)
I. Bishop Simplicius to John, bishop of Ravenna.

If there were any regard for ecclesiastical discipline, or if any priestly restraint were kept by you, punishable excesses would never be committed; and if you were not held back from them by any precept of the fathers' rules, you ought at least to have been recalled by the example of your predecessor of holy memory, who, though he had offended less by making a man a presbyter against his will, nevertheless suffered a fitting judgement for such a usurpation. Where did you learn these things which you committed against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory, not by election but by spite? You allowed him, with inexcusable violence, to be dragged to you and harassed, so that you imposed so great an honour on him not through calmness of mind but through madness, as it must be called. For such things could not have been done with soundness of counsel; we do not wish to magnify what was done, lest we be compelled to judge what it deserves: for he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power granted him. But one reason makes us milder in our sentence, which we preferred that you learn from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Projectus rather than publish it by our letter, on account of the disgrace. For our moderation has so restrained the scandal of which you are recognised as the author that my brother and fellow bishop Gregory, who, it is agreed, was not promoted but driven out, shall govern the church of Modena, having, as he asked, no case with you; and let him not refuse to embrace the spiritual fellowship which he ought not to have been allotted against his will; and if any business should perhaps arise for him, let our examination be sought by him or against him. We also provide for the needs which he is compelled to bear through your doing by this decision: that the estate which he records was given to him a year ago being given back and returned to the church of Ravenna, a property in the territory of Bologna with 30 solidi of free revenues be handed over without hesitation, namely for the term of his life, saving the right of ownership of the church of Ravenna, to which it will return after the death of the aforesaid. But if our decrees are not obeyed, you yourself can weigh what awaits the contumacious after transgression. And we give notice that if hereafter you presume anything of the kind, and perhaps think fit to make anyone, whether bishop, presbyter or deacon, against his will, you are to know that the ordinations of the church of Ravenna and of Aemilia will be taken from you. Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Severinus, man of clarissimus rank. (A.D. 481.)
II. Bishop Simplicius to the bishops Florentius, Equitius and Severus.

The report of your love has informed us, and the series of acts has made more fully known, that Gaudentius, priest of the church of Aufinum, has performed unlawful ordinations against the statutes of the canons and our precepts; and we order that all power of these be wholly taken from him. For we have written to Severus, our brother and fellow bishop, that, if it is necessary, he himself, having considered the rules of the Fathers, should discharge in the aforesaid church that office which the other is convicted of having abused: so that those who were unlawfully promoted by him be removed from the ecclesiastical ministries. At the same time also, concerning the revenues of the church or the offerings of the faithful, let him assure the man, who does not know what is fitting, that nothing is permitted him; but let only a fourth portion of these be left to him; let two [portions], to benefit the church buildings and the provision for strangers and the poor, be administered by the presbyter Onager at the peril of his own order; let the last be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each. But let the presumptuous man be compelled by the insistence of the aforesaid brother to restore the sacred vessels of the church which we have learned were alienated; and we have specially commanded him to press in this too, that he restore those three portions which he is said to have claimed for himself alone over three years. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, after the consulship of Leo Augustus. (A.D. 475.)
In the consulship of Flavius Boethius, man of clarissimus rank, on the third day before the Ides of March, in the Constantinian basilica, the venerable man Pope Felix presiding, together with

the deacons also standing by, Felix, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, presiding over the synod, said: Common is the sorrow and general the groaning, because we have learned that within Africa even bishops, presbyters and deacons have been rebaptized; a matter which has without doubt come also to the knowledge of your holiness. It is fitting for us to ordain what ought to be observed concerning this. Therefore, so that our judgement on this may be plain, let what has seemed good to us be read out. The deacon Anastasius read.
To the most beloved brothers in Christ Jesus, all the bishops established throughout the various provinces.

How in the regions of Africa the cunning of the devil has raged against the Christian people, and has burst out with manifold deception to the point that it has plunged not only the unwary common people but the priests themselves into the depths of death, there is no part of the world that has not groaned, no land that has not known. Hence, placed in great grief, we cannot disregard the peril of souls that are perishing and that are to be required of us; wherefore a fitting medicine must be applied to such wounds, lest a premature ease in curing profit nothing those caught by a deadly plague, or the ruin, treated too sluggishly, involve the wounded and the healers alike in the guilt of an unlawful cure. First, therefore, the profession of anyone coming to you and asking for a remedy must be carefully examined, and the person of the one deceived, so that a fitting medicine may be offered. And whoever, intending to make satisfaction to God through penance, rightly grieves that he has been rebaptized, let it be inquired whether he ran to this crime or came to it under compulsion. [Let him know] that he who deceives deceives himself, and that nothing is taken away through our leniency from the lofty judgement of the tribunal, to which those things are valid that are pious, true and just; and necessity is to be treated on a different reckoning from will. Worse, however, is the case of one who was perhaps enticed by a price to perish. For the enemy has left nothing untried; so that he may not be allowed to rejoice in his catch, help must be given to the ensnared, and the hunter's snare must be broken, so that for those who lament their fall in flight there may be a return to the hall they had left, by the moderation of justice as much as by the compunction of piety; and let them not perhaps be ashamed or reluctant to obey the appointed seasons of fasting and groaning, or to comply with the other precepts of a more wholesome observance, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud (James 4). If then whoever, laid low by grief at his fall, seeks to be raised up in Christ, let us, through the ministry of our dispensation (which it is fitting for your charity to follow, and which it is not lawful for anyone either to wish or to be able to overstep), treat with priestly vigour and humanity the case of him who, against the apostolic teaching, gave himself up to the repetition of a most ill-omened baptism, or of him who cunningly thought his consent should be excused by some arguments, so that in them faith (which, unless it is one, is already none) may, with the help of the Lord the judge, be restored to salvation without offence from our haste; because when the satisfaction of a sinner is prolonged by us, his mind is found, not without our praise and joy, the purer for pardon. And therefore remember that we hold this judgement concerning these matters: that, the distinction between sinners being kept, not all who have fallen be weighed in the same balance, since a heavier interest of chastisement must be exacted from one to whom the discipline of the Lord's house has been entrusted.

So then, to begin from the highest ranks of the Church: those who are established to have been bishops, presbyters or deacons, and who, whether perhaps willingly or under compulsion, have clearly made loss of that unique and saving washing, and have stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only by the gift of regeneration but also by the grace of the honour they had received, since it is established that no one could have come to a second dipping unless he had openly denied that he was a Christian and professed himself a pagan. Though this is to be execrated in all generally, in bishops, presbyters and deacons it is shown to be far more horrible even to hear and to speak of. But since the same Lord and Saviour is most merciful and wills no one to perish, it will be fitting that they lie in penance until the day of their departure, if they come to their senses, and that they by no means be present at the prayer not only of the faithful but not even of the catechumens; to them lay communion is to be restored at death, a matter which the care of a most approved priest must examine and carry out diligently.

Concerning clerics, however, and monks, or virgins of God, or laypeople, we command that this rule be kept which the synod of Nicaea established was to be kept regarding those who have lapsed or shall have lapsed: namely, that those who under no necessity, through no fear or danger of anything, impiously gave themselves up to heretics to be rebaptized, if they repent from the heart, shall be three years among the hearers, and for seven years shall lie among the penitents under the hands of the priests, and for two [more] shall by no means be admitted to the offerings, but shall be joined with the people only in prayer; and let him not be ashamed to bow his neck to God who did not fear to deny him. But if, being mortal, the end of life begins to press upon one within the bounds of the prescribed time, help must be given to him who implores it, and whether by the bishop who gave the penance, or by another who has nevertheless verified that it was given, or likewise by a presbyter, let viaticum not be denied to one departing from the world.

To boys, however, who are so called from puberty because they are still beardless, whether clerics or laypeople, or also to girls of like age, whom ignorance due to age supports, after being held for some time under the imposition of hands, communion is to be restored, and their penance is not to be awaited, since the rule exempts them from coercion; this we have prudently established, lest those for whom more or less of life remains amid the stain of earthly contagion should perhaps commit things to be repented of while they are still in penance. But if anyone, before the appointed time of penance, despaired of by the physicians or pressed by evident signs of death, receives the grace of communion and recovers, let us keep in his case what the canons of Nicaea ordained, that he be held among those who communicate in prayer only, until the span of time assigned to him is completed.

Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, because (as the same holy canons ordained) the case is not unlike that of one who has in any way abjured Christ, whom he once confessed: let them be three years among the hearers, and afterwards be allowed to pray with the catechumens, to receive the grace of catholic communion through the imposition of hands. Excepting indeed only bishops, presbyters and deacons, who, as we have already said, are to be reconciled only at the time of their death, we decree that the rest, whether clerics, or monks or nuns, or laypeople, persons of either sex, who are established to have undergone the repetition of baptism compelled by violence and dangers, or who by some fabrication have said they are not bound by the guilt of this crime, shall continue in penance for three years, and through the imposition of hands be received into the fellowship of the sacrament. This being kept in every respect: that none of those who at any age have been baptized or rebaptized elsewhere than in the catholic Church shall ever be permitted at all to enter the ecclesiastical service; it ought to be enough for them that they have been received into the number of catholics; since any prelate who violates this will be seen to pass judgement on his own order and communion, as will he who does not remove one of these whom he knows to have crept into the clerical ministry. But it must above all be taken care of, and provided with every caution, that none of our brothers and fellow bishops, or even presbyters, receive in another's city or diocese a penitent, or one placed under the hand of a priest, or one who says he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter, whether a presbyter in a parish or a bishop in a city; for this, if neglected through any connivance, touches with guilt also the clerics who dwell in the places where this has been less carefully observed. These things therefore having been duly arranged and brought by our deliberation to the knowledge of your churches, it is fitting that you obey; and although nothing seems lacking in them for the restoration of souls, yet if something new, which may have escaped us, has been revealed to anyone, according to the blessed apostle Paul (1 Cor. 14), the former being silent, let him confidently put it forward, because the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills, especially when his own cause is being treated; nor shall we be reluctant to hear, and if anything has been omitted, not arrogantly to refuse it but reasonably to ordain it. Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Dynamius and Sifidius, men of clarissimus rank. (A.D. 488.)

After the consulship of Paulinus, man of clarissimus rank, on the Kalends of March, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, with the most blessed Pope Symmachus presiding over the synod, Fulgentius the archdeacon said: Your Beatitude, having sent out letters of authority through the provinces before this, has frequently convoked a synod of the priests of Italy, whose presence is seen to be set before your eyes; now let your Beatitude deign to order in a manner fit for deliberation the things that pertain to the security of the Church, or to the peace or concord of the whole Church. It was acclaimed by all the bishops and presbyters: Hear us, Christ, life to Symmachus; this was said ten times. [May you hold] his see and years; this was said eight times. We ask that you do it; this was said ten times.

Symmachus, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: Our concern for the security of the Church has specially gathered this council of your charity, disregarding the harshness of winter, so that, by sharing our deliberation together, we may for the future cut away firmly and vigorously the canvassing for the episcopate, the uncertainty of confusion, and the popular tumult which, as is known, arose through underhand dealing; and so that we may therefore take care for the time to come that neither the subversion of discipline nor the boldness of the presumptuous may be eager to attempt the like; and that we may deliberate with equal grant [of voice], namely ordaining by express decisions what ought to be observed concerning the ordination of the Roman bishop. All the bishops and presbyters said: We ask that it be done; this was said ten times. We ask that scandals be cut away; this was said nine times. We ask that canvassing be extinguished; this was said twelve times. Hear us, Christ, life to Symmachus; this was said six times. [May you hold] his see and years; this was said five times. Let it be done at once; this was said ten times.

Bishop Symmachus said: Since your fraternity has spurred on the care of our provision with its exhortations, and shows an equal mind concerning the tranquillity of the Church out of regard for our God, as we said before, now that deliberation has been held at present, make known by all your opinions what is approved, [the decrees] which are to be read out in this venerable council through the officials of the Church. And when they had risen, and a little later had sat down again, Aemilianus the notary made public the decrees of the synod.

I. On account of the frequent canvassing of certain persons, and the stripping of the Church, and the clashing of the people, which the troublesome greed of those improperly desiring the episcopate has produced, so that so pernicious a presumption may be extinguished in future times, the holy synod has established that if any presbyter, or deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, should attempt either to lend his subscription for the Roman pontificate, or to promise it by a note, or to give an oath, or indeed to pledge any vote, or to deliberate and decide on this matter in private gatherings held for the purpose, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his rank or of communion. The whole synod rose and acclaimed: Hear us, Christ, life to Symmachus; said ten times. Here is peace with Symmachus; said fifteen times. [May you hold] his see and years; said eight times. With equal severity is to be struck the one who, while this pontiff is living (as has been said), is convicted of having canvassed in any way, or indeed of having attempted it, all those guilty of this fault being alike punished with the penalty of anathema.
Bishop Symmachus said: Does this decision then please the whole body, and is it acknowledged and approved by all? The whole synod said: It pleases, and let what pleases all be done.

II. If (God forbid) the death of the pope should occur unexpectedly, so that he cannot decide beforehand concerning the election of his successor, as was approved above, then if the choice of the whole ecclesiastical order inclines to one person, let the one elected be consecrated bishop. But if, as tends to happen, the inclinations of those among whom a contest has arisen begin to differ, let the opinion of the majority prevail; yet in such a way that he shall lose his priesthood who, taken by a promise, has decided on the election not by sound judgement. The synod said: It pleases; this was said ten times.

III. Moreover, on account of the hidden frauds and secret snares of conspiracies, which the sentence of this strictness pursues, if anyone brings to the knowledge of the Church the plans of those who, against this synod, have engaged in canvassing for the pontificate, and proves them by reasonable proof, [even if he was] a participant in such an action, let him not only be cleared of all guilt, but also be relieved with a reward that is not unworthy. The whole synod rose and acclaimed: All [these] please; and added: Hear us, Christ, life to Symmachus; this was said thirteen times. We ask that they be kept so; this was said ten times. We pray that no one come to the Roman episcopate otherwise from now on; this was said ten times. We ask that you confirm our decrees; this was said ten times.

Symmachus, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: The present acts will take in your acclamations and the judgement of the synod. And he added: What a deliberation befitting religion and peace has established for calming the errors of long-standing presumption and the diseased ills hostile to church affairs by which the universal Church was afflicted, shall obtain perpetual firmness, so that, by the gift of God, who is known to be the guardian of good things, the synodal ordinance may be in force, and whoever, without distinction of any person, presumes to come [otherwise] shall be punished with the strictness laid down above.
