In the consulship of Flavius Avienus the younger, man of clarissimus rank, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, the venerable man Pope Symmachus presiding, together with the venerable men the bishops,
the presbyters also sitting with them:

and the deacons also standing by, Anastasius, Hormisdas, Joannes and Agapetus. Symmachus, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: I. Your fraternity has indeed done well, obeying the ecclesiastical laws under fear of the divine judgement, in defining what had to be decreed, and you have reached the full measure of justice, since it embraces everything sufficiently and its fullness needs no addition, above all concerning the clerics whom love of domination has seized and has made to spurn the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline, who for that reason were established before you to have made a schism; yet you have not denied them, as was fitting, the mercy which God commands to be shown to all, unless the hardness of their heart should bring punishment upon itself by despising the remedies offered; their excesses it is difficult to recount. One thing, however, which occurs to me, I do not delay to make known to your venerable order. They said, among other things, that Basilius of illustrious memory had drawn up a certain document, supposedly out of love for the property of the Church, at which no bishop of the Roman Church was present and which none subscribed, through whom it could have obtained lawful validity. So that I may not argue about a matter on which your council can judge, let it be sought out and brought forward, so that by reading it you may learn what kind of standing it can have. The holy synod replied: Let it be brought forward, so that it may be known what kind of thing it is; and while it was saying this, the deacon Hormisdas read it out. II. When they had sat together at [the church of] the blessed apostle Peter, the exalted and most eminent man Basilius, praetorian prefect and patrician, acting also on behalf of the most excellent king Odoacer, said: Although it is a matter of our concern and of our religion that concord in the Church be chiefly preserved in the election of a bishop, so that the condition of the city may not be called into doubt through an occasion of sedition, nevertheless you remember the admonition of our most blessed man Pope Simplicius, which we ought always to have before our eyes, that this was enjoined on us under solemn charge: because of that uproar and the harm to the venerable Church, if it should happen that he passed from this light, the election of anyone should not be held without our consultation. And while he was reading, Cresconius, bishop of the Church of the city of Tuder, rising from the assembly, said: Here let the holy synod weigh how, passing over the religious persons who chiefly have the care of so great a pontiff, they brought [the matter] into their own power. That this is against the canons is evident. Again the deacon Hormisdas read: So that the venerable Church should suffer no confusion or loss, we are surprised that anything was attempted with us passed over, since nothing ought to have been undertaken while our priest was living. Therefore, if it pleases your greatness or holiness, let us preserve intact, with religious care, everything that concerns the election of the future bishop, setting forth in particular this law, which we decree for ourselves and our heirs out of the devotion of a Christian mind:

that never shall any estate, whether rural or urban, or the ornaments or vessels of the churches, those that exist now or those that shall come under the rights of the churches by any titles whatever, [be alienated]; if he who is now to be ordained bishop by common election, and those who shall follow in future ages, should wish to alienate them by any title or device whatever, let it be judged ineffective and void, and let there be anathema on him who does it, on him who consents, and on him who receives. Maximus, bishop of the Church of Bleda, said: Now let the holy synod deign to declare: was it lawful for a layman to pronounce anathema against the ecclesiastical order? Or, if a layman could pronounce anathema on a priest, [could he] also decree against the canons what it was not his place [to decree]? Say, what do you think of me? Was it lawful for a layman to give law? The holy synod said: It was not lawful; and it added: Read what follows. The deacon Hormisdas read: And let him who has obtained a rural or urban estate under ecclesiastical right know that he is protected by no law or prescription, but if either he who alienated it, or those who follow him, should with a contrary will try to recover an estate alienated in this way, let him who obtained it restore it with its fruits. And while he was reading, Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Venusia, rising from the assembly, said: Let it be read through. The deacon Hormisdas read:

It is resolved that this penalty also applies to the heirs and successors of those who receive. In this matter let any of the clerics have free power to object. For it is unjust, and like sacrilege, that what each person has contributed, or at any rate bequeathed, to the venerable Church for the sake of the poor, either for the salvation or for the repose of their souls, should be transferred elsewhere by those whom it most befitted to preserve it. Clearly, whatever in jewels, or gold and silver, and also in garments, shall seem less suited to the uses or adornment of the Church, which cannot be preserved and last long, let it be sold at a fair valuation, and let the distribution [of the proceeds] be applied religiously. And when it had been read, Laurentius of the Church of Milan said: This document could bind no pontiff of the city of Rome, because it was not lawful for a layman to have any power of decreeing in the Church apart from the Roman pope, a layman for whom remains the obligation to obey, not the authority to command; above all since neither did the Roman pope subscribe, nor is the assent of any metropolitan read [in it] according to the canons. Petrus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said: It is evident that the document which has been made public in our assembly stands with no force, because it does not agree with the canons and appears to have been conceived by a lay person, above all because no prelate of the apostolic see is shown to have been present at it or to have confirmed it with his own subscription. Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said: The document which has been read in the council of priests is established by the clearest proofs to be invalid. First, because, against the rules of the Fathers, it appears to have been made by laymen, however religious, to whom no power of disposing anything about ecclesiastical property is ever read to have been granted; secondly, because it is shown to have been confirmed by the subscription of no prelate of the apostolic see. For if the holy Fathers decreed that whatever the priests of any province, holding a council within their own bounds, attempted without the authority of their metropolitan bishop must be void, how much more is it beyond doubt that what is known to have been presumed by laymen when there was no prelate in the apostolic see, who, holding by the prerogative of the blessed merit of the apostle Peter the primacy of the priesthood throughout the whole world, is accustomed to give validity to synodal decrees, even with some bishops consenting (who nonetheless could not prejudice the pontiff by whom they are shown to be consecrated), lacks force, and can in no way be counted among ecclesiastical statutes.

III. The holy synod said: Although, according to the statements of our venerable brothers Laurentius, Petrus, Eulalius, Cresconius, Maximus and Stephanus, it is not held uncertain among us either that this document is of no weight, yet even if it could stand on some reasoning, it was fitting that in the synodal assembly it be in every way deprived of force and brought to nothing by the provident sentence of your beatitude, so that there should not remain a precedent for any laymen, however religious or powerful, in any city whatever, to presume in any way to decree anything about ecclesiastical property, the care of disposing of which is taught to have been committed by God unquestionably to priests alone.

Bishop Symmachus said: Now, since God has granted me your longed-for presence, on whatever occasion, I wish, if it pleases [you], that a measure be made firm which I believe befits ecclesiastical property, so that all whom vain fury has stirred up against me may know that I strive for nothing more than that what has been committed to me by God for stewardship may be kept safe, but [a measure] which also ought to be welcome to any successors who fear God, and pertains to the safeguarding of the ecclesiastical patrimony. The holy synod said: We know that your foresight attends to what is necessary, and therefore it is in your power to arrange what is to follow.

Symmachus, bishop of the catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: Great reverence is indeed owed to the venerable and priestly calling, whose part is to arrange what is right from zeal, not from compulsion. But since in some who seek what belongs to others, avarice, the mother of vices, having cast off the barriers of honour, thinks that everything which is possible is expedient, and so, while it gapes after plunder, abuses the patience of the heavenly mercy; while heaven governs [all] and awaits correction, they consider themselves not bound by judgements, and it is plain that with certain people the delay of the divine sentence turns into an occasion for seizing. But for us, whom pastoral care binds, and the account to be rendered of the ecclesiastical property entrusted to us for stewardship, it is needful to extend our solicitude not only to the present but also to the ages to come, lest it turn to the harm of our soul if those who are able [to abuse it] should transgress out of the liberty of presuming [left] by their innocence of statutes, when both we and our successors can be supported by religious power, serving the ecclesiastical laws.

IV. These things being weighed, therefore, with regard for our God, we decree by a lasting decree that no prelate of the apostolic see, from the present day for as long as, by the Lord's disposing, the saving doctrine of the catholic faith shall remain, may transfer a rural estate, of whatever size it be, great or small, to anyone's rights by perpetual alienation or exchange, nor shall anyone be excused on the plea of necessity. Since indeed what we speak of is not a personal matter, let no one, cleric or layman, keep what he has received on this pretext; nor may rights be given to any in usufruct, nor retained if given, except to clerics, captives and strangers, so that no occasion for bad dealing may be supplied, since other ways are reserved for that generosity. Only houses situated in any cities, whose condition must be maintained at no small expense, may be exchanged, if it should happen that they are given away, on receiving revenues at a fair valuation, and with fear of the divine judgement.

V. We wish also that the guardians of the churches throughout all the titles of the Roman city, whether they are presbyters or whoever they may be, be bound by the same law, since it is wicked to say that a man of the second order in the Church should not be held by the obligation by which the supreme pontiff binds himself through the love of Christ. Whoever, however, forgetful of God and unmindful of this decree, by which we wish the priests of the Roman city to be bound with religious ties, offends against the present constitution and attempts to alienate by perpetual right anything belonging to the titles, or to the Church mentioned above, in any manner (except gold, silver or gems, and also vestments, if there are [any] or if they have been added, [and] any movables not pertaining to the divine adornments, houses alone being excepted under the aforesaid condition), let the donor, alienator and seller be punished with the loss of his rank.

VI. Moreover, whoever has sought or received [such property], or whoever of the presbyters, deacons or defensors has subscribed for the giver, let him be struck with the anathema with which an angry God strikes souls; and let the receiver or the subscriber among the persons comprised above, that is, those whom we have judged are to be struck with anathema, share in the established penalty, the punishment which we laid down for the alienator being kept. Unless perhaps both the alienator, by reclaiming, and he who received, by swift restitution, have looked to their own interests.

VII. But if anyone, with too little care for his soul, should perhaps neglect the remedy offered, then beyond those kinds of penalties which are written above, any document that has been drawn up against right shall be deprived of all force (although it had none from the beginning). But let it also be lawful for any ecclesiastical persons to raise a voice of objection and to be supported by ecclesiastical authority, so that one may reclaim another's property together with its fruits; nor may [the holder] shield himself with any obstacle before the tribunal of Christ, because he scatters against right, without any regard for piety, what was left by religious souls for the sustenance of the poor. We wish the law of this constitution, however, to be observed in the apostolic see only, while in all the churches throughout the provinces the custom is kept according to the consideration of souls which their rulers see to befit the purpose of religion. And they subscribed.
I, Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the Roman Church, have subscribed to this constitution made by us.
I, Caelius Laurentius, bishop of the holy Church of Milan, have subscribed to this constitution made by the venerable pope Symmachus.
I, Petrus, bishop of the catholic Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this constitution made by the venerable pope Symmachus.
I, Eulalius, bishop of the holy Church of Syracuse, have subscribed to this constitution made by the venerable pope Symmachus.

In the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, man of clarissimus rank, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. The holy synod, assembled in the city of Rome from various regions by order of the most glorious king Theodoric, said in the name of Christ: When royal authority had ordered the priests to convene from various provinces to the city of Rome, so that the holy council might judge the charges which were said to be brought by his adversaries against the venerable pope Symmachus, prelate of the apostolic see, the bishops of Liguria, Aemilia and Venetia, whom the very route of their journey brought into the presence of the prince, felt the necessity of consulting the king as to what cause had required that they, broken by age and weak in bodily infirmity, be assembled. The aforesaid most pious king replied, with the disposition of good conduct, that many horrible things had been reported to him about the acts of pope Symmachus, and that they ought to be dealt with in a synod, [to see] whether the charge of his enemies was established as true by judgement. The aforementioned bishops, upon whom the occasion of pleading lay, suggested that he himself who was said to be accused ought to have convoked the synod, knowing that first the merit or primacy of the apostle Peter, and then, following the command of the Lord, the authority of the venerable councils, had conferred on his see a singular power in the churches, and that hardly any instance could readily be cited to attest that the prelate of the said see had been subject to the judgement of his inferiors in a similar case. But the most powerful prince indicated that the pope himself also had shown by letters his will for the gathering of the synod. The pages which, it was agreed, had been sent by him were requested of his clemency; he arranged that they be given to the priests without delay, together with whatever had been done in the same matter, [and] by God's guidance [we] arrived at Rome from various parts of lands and regions. And while in the venerable assembly there was discussion of beginning the business, as the cause of the proceedings demanded, the holy pope Symmachus, as was his care, swiftly entered the basilica of Julius, in which the gathering of bishops was, and gave thanks to the most clement king for the summoning of the synod, and testified that the thing had come about as he desired. Thus the cause which, because the council was not yet confirmed, was bringing sadness to the minds of the priests was cut away; he professed, in the presence of all the bishops who had gathered there, that he gave authority to the assembly being convened, as the ecclesiastical statutes required, hoping that the visitor, who had been requested by part of the clergy or by certain laymen against religion, against the statutes of the ancients and against the rules of our forebears, would by order of the bishops withdraw at the very outset, as befitted the holy calling; and that all that he had lost through the suggestions of his enemies would be restored to his power by the honourable council, and that the prelate of so great a place should first be lawfully restored to his former state, and then come to the case, and, if it seemed right, answer the propositions of the accusers. The thing seemed worthy to the greatest number of the priests, and worthy to obtain effect. Yet the synod did not presume to decree anything without the king's knowledge; but the just suggestion, through the negligence of the envoys, did not earn a reply according to our wishes. Pope Symmachus was ordered by the king's commands to contend in debate with his assailants before the recovery of the patrimony or of the churches which he had lost; and he, as to the privileges of his power and what he had submitted (as far as we justly judge) for the amendment of conscience, was unwilling to resume them even on this occasion. But while the synod was gathered in the Jerusalem basilica of the Sessorian palace, it seemed good to some priests that the libellus which the accusers had prepared, who daily made their appeals with seditions, should be received by the synod; and when it was received there were two things in it which were either hostile to the truth or, as is shown, repugnant to those assembled in their ecclesiastical purpose. One, that they said the crimes of the aforesaid pope Symmachus had been established in the king's knowledge; which [the king] declared false, for he would not have committed it to a hearing as a new case if he knew that [Symmachus], convicted of wrongdoing on his conscience, awaited only sentence. The other, that they said they could convict him through slaves concerning the things they alleged, adding that he himself should hand over the slaves, by whom, as they asserted, he could be overcome in judgement. This was hostile to the canons and to the public laws themselves, since the statutes of the fathers had decreed that those whom the laws of the world do not admit to accusation should not be granted licence to speak in a hearing or to accuse anyone. And while what should be done amid these things was being discussed, the aforesaid pope was on his way to plead his case; and as he came he was so handled by the onrushing crowds of his rivals that the attack itself brought about the death of many presbyters who were with him; and the illustrious man count Aligernus and the sublime men Gudila and Vedeulf, majordomos of the royal house, saw the traces of wounds still fresh, and that he betook himself back to the precincts of the blessed apostle Peter, from where he had set out. These things having been done, and affairs disturbed by manifold confusion, we again had recourse to the prince's justice, knowing that the Lord's own divinity governs what it has provided for the governance of Italy, and we laid everything before his clemency in a series of reports, as the matter required. We informed [him] also that the oft-named pope, after the attack which he and his [people] had suffered, had been asked whether he again had the will to go out to judgement, but that he had alleged through bishops sent [by him] that, in his desire to clear himself, his eminence had humbled itself beyond what the canons granted him, [and] by how many dangers they had nearly been overwhelmed; that the lord king had [the power] to do what he wished, [but] that he himself in the meantime, resisting, could not be compelled against justice by the canonical statutes. To this the most serene king, God inspiring him, answered thus: that it lay within the synod's discretion to prescribe what should be followed in so great a matter, and that nothing about ecclesiastical affairs pertained to him beyond reverence; entrusting also to the power of the bishops that, whether they wished to hear the proposed matter or not, they should decide what they thought more useful, provided that by the provision of the venerable council there was peace in the city of Rome for all Christians, [peace] by which, when it is justly offered, the commands of God are fulfilled. Recognising [that God had given] a ruler to his Italy, [and] that no other labour remained for us except to exhort the dissenters to concord with the humility of our calling, since one thing remained in so great a matter by which we might obey God as well as the holy will of the prince, we invite the most ample senate, sending such a delegation as was fitting, admonishing and instructing [them] that the causes of God are to be committed to his own judgement, who is able to kill the body and send the soul into Gehenna (Matt. 10); who says, Vengeance is mine, and I will repay (Ezek. 9); before whom conscience is naked (Rom. 12), from whom hidden things are not concealed; that prudent men ought to consider how much had happened improperly and prejudicially at the beginning of this business, and that by this which they themselves called remission we do not open but close the way to sins, since we reserve what was alleged for a greater judgement; instructing them that, since through us Christ has made himself known to them (John 10), it is the part not of the sheep but of the shepherd to foresee the wolf's ambushes; especially since in the said case error had entangled many, [who] deigned to acknowledge themselves and to make satisfaction to God. And that the members of the Church ought not to be scattered further on this occasion, but rather sustained through gentleness, as Paul, the master of good work, had instructed us (2 Tim. 4), saying that very many are to be healed by patience and teaching. And whoever are thought guilty and entangled in grave sins (though there is no one who is without fault, as the apostle John testifies (1 John 1): If I say that I have no sin, I am a liar), these are rather sustained by the pressures of men, and the divine judgements are suspended [so that they may be] terrified by these sufferings; especially since the things which we set out above, among others, concerning the authority of the see stood in the way, because what its possessor of old, the blessed Peter, merited passed into the nobility of the possession, and gives you ancient renown, [and] grants it by Christ's endowment to [its] rulers; crying out that it is written through the prophet in the person of God (Isa. 50): Is my hand not able to consume those who have erred? Admonishing [them] of these same things very often, as was fitting, that they should depart, holding [to this] intention, and should not dispute our deed, which God had inspired, in accordance with the prince's mandate, but follow it, as befitted sons of the Church, and not contend under this pretext, so that the harms to the Church should grow. This matter required to be relieved with haste, and the necessity of this speed lay upon us, and that of obedience upon them; especially as we see almost all the people inseparably adhering to his communion, for whom no small care spurred us, lest they fall into any error. These things having been set forth, with solemn invocation of our God we decree, constrained by consideration of these necessities and of religion, and all things in the case having been weighed by heavenly inspiration, that pope Symmachus, prelate of the apostolic see, assailed by propositions of this kind, as far as regards men (since it is agreed that the whole has been left to the divine decision because of the obstacles to the case designated above), be immune and free, and let him deliver the divine mysteries to the Christian people without any objection regarding the charges, in all his churches pertaining to the right of his see, because we have recognised that he could not be bound by the assault of his assailants, for the reasons designated above. Therefore, according to the prince's commands, which grant this to our power, we restore to him whatever is of ecclesiastical right within the holy city of Rome or outside it, reserving the whole case to the judgement of God; we exhort all to receive holy communion from him, as the matter requires, and to be mindful of God and of their own souls, because he is both a lover of peace and is himself peace, who warns, My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14; Matt. 10). And affirming that peace is to be confirmed in every city, he says that the peacemakers are blessed (ibid. 5). Whoever either does not admit these things from our instruction (which we do not expect) or believes that they can be revoked, let him see that in the divine judgement he will render account for his contempt, as we trust in God. Concerning the clerics of the said pope who some time ago departed from their bishop against the rules and made a schism, we have decreed that this be done: that mercy follow them when they make satisfaction to their bishop, and that they may rejoice to be restored to ecclesiastical offices, because our Lord and Redeemer rejoices when lost sheep are found from their wandering, and the heavenly healer extends a father's generosity over the runaway son (Luke 15). But any cleric who, after this form approved by us, presumes to celebrate masses in any place consecrated to God in the Roman Church without the knowledge of pope Symmachus, while he lives, let him be struck down as a schismatic by the canonical statutes. Let it suffice to have declared these things sincerely, with God's knowledge. And they subscribed.
I, Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed to this our statute, in which we have committed the whole case to the judgement of God.
I, Petrus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this our statute, in which we have committed the whole case to the judgement of God.

With what zeal we have always been, and are, for reconciling the views of those who cultivate the catholic faith, so that all may venerate with the same mind the indivisible light of the Trinity, we are known to have made plain: now by sending to your beatitude of our own accord, for this very purpose, an envoy, Gratus, a man of spectabilis rank, master of the bureau, so that a remedy might at last be found for the discords of those contending in various ways; now by receiving with ready and willing affection the most religious men whom your apostolic see believed should be sent as mediators of unity. For indeed we looked upon them with joyful eyes as if they were peace itself, and judged that they should be embraced with outstretched hands. Moreover we shall arrange with every effort that the venerable Church of Constantinople, and many others too, accept your wishes, not only in other matters but also in removing from the sacred diptychs the names which you have most especially demanded be removed. But there have been some cities and Churches, both of Pontus and of Asia, and especially of the East, whose clergy or people, though tried with every threat and persuasion, have nevertheless in no way been bent to take away and reject the names of bishops whose reputation flourished among them; rather they reckon life harsher than death if they should condemn the dead in whose life, while they were still living, they gloried. What then are we to do with obstinacy of this kind, which neither obeys what it is told and so far despises torments that it judges it a fine and festive thing for itself to depart from the body before departing from its religious resolve? To us indeed it seems necessary to act more gently and more mercifully; and if these [qualities] are not now to be found in your holiness, they cannot be found in any other either. For we did not take up the libellus desiring blood and punishments (which is grievous even to say), nor so that the desires for concord should remain unfulfilled over a small difference, but in order to extend, by whatever course we can, the joining of the members of the Church. Which then will be better: for the sake of lesser things to have such great multitudes wholly opposed to us, or, by granting and remitting small things, to have the greater things, which are to be sought by every means, set right, so that what could not be achieved in everything may at least be secured in the necessary parts? We therefore ask pardon for the names, not of Acacius, not of either Peter, not of Dioscorus or Timothy, whose names the letters of your holiness delivered to us contained, but of those whom episcopal reverence has honoured in other cities; and this excepting the cities where your beatitude's libellus has already been fully admitted, unless your benevolence decides that this part too is to be corrected more gently. Nor indeed does the matter lack a judgement of the apostolic see, so that it should be called not so much a pardon as a definition already deliberated and examined. For Anastasius of most religious memory, the summit of your Church, had openly and plainly laid down, when he wrote about this same business to our predecessor, that it was enough for those seeking peace if only the name of Acacius were passed over in silence. Therefore he follows the earlier decisions of your see who judges that not all memorials of the dead are to be scorned; so that it would be held unworthy and unfitting if your mildness, gentler towards all, not only the dead but also the living, were not published to every end of the earth. And indeed we would not doubt that it will be so pleasing to you that the world will at once be made happier by a peaceful reply. Let your holiness also remember what we wrote some time ago, that petitions had been sent to us from the East containing their will and decision, in which they show that they will firmly persist, and from which they think they must on no account desist. This document, then, in accordance with our promises, we have now rightly judged should be sent to you through John, a most reverend man, a bishop; so that its tenor, once admitted also by your see, may serve to gather and unite the venerable Churches everywhere, and especially that of Jerusalem, to which all pay such favour, as to the mother of the Christian name, that no one dares to separate himself from her. It is fitting, therefore, that your holiness declare your own consent also in a letter, so that, when it is known to all and made plain that the tenor of this same document is also approved by you and firmly kept, the world may be happier. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September at Chalcedon, in the consulship of Rusticius; received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship written above. (Year of Christ 520.)

II. To the God-beloved and most pious emperor, Augustus from God, and most Christian prince Justin: a petition and supplication from the clergy of Jerusalem, of Antioch and of Syria Secunda, and from the abbots and landowners of the province of Syria.

'Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation,' cries out the prophet Isaiah and proclaims (Isa. 12), clearly showing the evangelical truths and preachings to be the springs of salvation, from which the blessed apostles, and those who were their disciples in succession, and the wise teachers of the Church, drawing the saving water of faith, have watered the whole holy Church of God, which, supported on the rock of the chief of the apostles and keeping the right and unbending confession, confidently cries out with him at all times to the only-begotten Son of God, saying: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' (Matt. 16). Having received this saving confession from the four holy synods, which are honoured by the evangelical precepts, we have never, by the grace of Christ, strayed from the right doctrines handed down to us, as the proof of events testifies and as our constancy in the faith in time of necessity demonstrates. If therefore, as Christians, we are partakers in the account of the faith, we hasten most piously both to the common peace and to unity, and we make our faith, which we received from the beginning, manifest to your piety through this our declaration, so that it may be known that we both concur in peace and, with God's help, do not turn aside from the right faith, but execrate every heresy alike: not only the Eutychianists and the Acephali, but also the Nestorians and those who worship a man we hate with all our soul and anathematize. We, lord most Christian emperor, as was said above, having also been baptized from the beginning into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and believing, adore one essence of God in three subsistences, according to the teaching and creed of the holy Fathers, believing in one God the Father almighty, and in one our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten, God the Word, and likewise in one Holy Spirit. And in accordance with this divine teaching we also understand and receive the definition promulgated by the holy synod of Chalcedon, confessing and believing that one subsistence or person, which the holy synod itself proclaimed in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, undivided and unconfused, God the Word and our Lord Jesus Christ, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. For if, as has been said, we accept one God in three subsistences, and the Father was not incarnate, nor the Holy Spirit, but God the Word was incarnate and became man, he is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity according to the property of sonship. So then, believing according to the aforesaid four holy synods, we do not refuse to confess also, according to God the Word, the birth according to the flesh. Hence the holy Virgin is believed to be properly the Mother of God, since she brought forth the Son who is by nature and in truth of one essence with the Father, God the Word, become man from her through an unchangeable nature; and confessing two natures in Christ united by essence or subsistence, as in the person or subsistence of one, we neither take away their difference or property after the union, nor have we been taught to divide them into two persons and subsistences through the union. And we know the same only-begotten Son of God, both before his incarnation and after, to be the same God and at once man, passible in the flesh, impassible in the godhead, circumscribed in body, uncircumscribed in spirit, the same earthly and heavenly, whom the world received as man and could not contain as God, mortal and immortal, the difference of the natures nowhere being taken away, nor dividing the union by essence. For this is truly the great mystery of piety: that God the Word, one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, incarnate and become man, is known and adored in both natures, of divinity and humanity, undivided and unconfused, undergoing no conversion or change, but preserving in himself the property of each nature in one person. For the sake of this faith, therefore, receiving and keeping the aforesaid holy synods, we anathematize all who at any time or in any way have written anything against them, especially John Aegeates, who as a Nestorian spewed out many blasphemies against the said holy synod of Chalcedon, likewise condemning also Timothy surnamed Aelurus, as a Eutychianist barking against it with his followers. Thus, then, with God's help we have always believed and still believe; and for this reason we have offered this declaration to your piety. For it has deigned to order us to set out our own understanding and how we think concerning the sound faith, because certain heretics, while they hasten to conceal their own evil faith, try to disparage our freedom in Christ and our right faith. We therefore beseech your clemency that it should take care for the perfect union of the holy Churches, so that the unity which has been made with God's help, and the peace, may not henceforth be disturbed by any kindling of occasion, reasonable or unreasonable. May the God of all fulfil your pious desire, to his glory and the good order of the commonwealth.

III. Among the matters concerning the unity of the Church, for whose sake God chose your clemency's rule, which you set down in your letter, the venerable emperor's care for the faith, to which you declare yourselves devoted in many ways, added this as well: that the petitions of certain persons, to be brought to the notice of my humility, should be attached. From these I might learn what question had arisen, or, to remove the doubt in the consultation put forward, a reply suited to religious knowledge might be returned by me. I read everything with fitting care. Although it could have been enough for a full reply if I wrote back only what was defined by the ancients, yet, to repay the devotion of your religious purpose, I believed I should not withhold the service of my own words as well, although concerning the poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches as they emerged the fathers' instruction omitted [nothing]: the synodal decrees, agreeing as one, forestalled almost all the impieties together with the inventors of such abominable dogmas. Nor, once such dreadful seeds of faithlessness had been cut off, is there any further room either to believe that Christ our Lord was without the reality of flesh, or [to deny] that he came forth as God and man from the undefiled fruitfulness of his mother's womb. For the one, by denying the dispensation by which we have been saved, would make it void as far as lay in him; the other, with a contrary opinion but a like impiety, would cut off the divine power in the same Lord Jesus Christ from true lowliness. The one did not remember that Christ showed his flesh to be touched (Luke 24); the other did not remember the Gospel, which says that the Word was made flesh (John 1). In his ears the Lord's voice should have sounded unceasingly, by which he said and taught (John 3): No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. These things have often been set out in many judgements of our predecessors; but your clemency will not be able to receive them with distaste when repeated, though they have been said before, nor are we ashamed to go back over what was preached by our predecessors. For it is not possible for there to be diversity of preaching where there is one form of truth; nor will it be judged out of place if, with those with whom we agree in faith, we also concur in doctrine. Let the synodal decrees, and the ordinances of blessed Pope Leo which agree with the sacred faith, be read again to the pious ears of your gentleness: you will find in them the same things that you review in ours. What then is there, after that fountain of faithful statutes, that any inquirer, however curious, might seek further, provided he keeps within the bounds of the faith? There is no need either of addition to what is full or of instruction for what is perfect, unless perhaps someone wishes to doubt rather than believe, to contend rather than know, to follow doubtful things rather than keep the decrees. For if God is Trinity, that is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, yet God is one, as the lawgiver expressly says (Deut. 6): Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one, whoever holds otherwise must either divide the godhead into many, or ascribe the passion specifically to the very essence of the Trinity. And this (far be it from the minds of the faithful) is either to bring in many gods after the manner of profane paganism, or to transfer perceptible suffering to that nature which is foreign to all suffering. The holy Trinity is one thing: it is not multiplied in number, it does not grow by increase, and it cannot either be grasped by understanding or, in that it is God, be separated by division. Who then would try to thrust a profane division upon that secret of the eternal and impenetrable substance, which no nature even of invisible creatures has been able to search out, and to bring divine and hidden mysteries back to the reckoning of human custom? Let us adore the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the undivided substance of the Trinity, distinctly, incomprehensible and inexpressible; where, if the account of the persons admits number, yet the unity does not lose the singularity of the essence; yet in such a way that we keep what is proper to the divine nature and keep what is proper to each person, so that neither is the singularity of the godhead engendered by the persons, nor is what is proper to the names transferred to the essence. Great and incomprehensible is the mystery of the holy Trinity. God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, an undivided Trinity; and yet it is known that it is proper to the Father to beget the Son; proper to the Son of God to be born of the Father, equal to the Father; it is known also what is proper to the Holy Spirit, namely to proceed from the Father and the Son under one substance of godhead. And it is proper to the Son of God that, according to what is written, in the last times the Word should become flesh and dwell among us (1 Pet. 1; John 1), both natures being so united within the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, without any confusion, that he who was Son of God before all ages became son of man, and was born in time after the manner of man, opening his mother's womb at birth and, by the power of his godhead, not undoing his mother's virginity. A mystery plainly worthy of God being born: that he kept the birth free of corruption who made the conception to be without seed, keeping what was from the Father and showing forth what he took from his mother. For how else was he, lying in a manger, seen in heaven; wrapped in swaddling cloths, adored by the magi; brought forth among animals, announced by angels; scarcely out of infancy, proclaiming mystical teachings with no one to instruct him; amid the first beginnings of his boyhood years, producing signs of heavenly powers? For the same is God and man, not, as the unbelievers say, by introducing a fourth person, but the Son of God himself is God and man, the same is power and weakness, lowliness and majesty, redeeming and sold, set on the cross and bestowing the kingdom of heaven. He was so far of our weakness that he could be killed, so far of innate power that he could not be consumed by death. He was buried according as he willed as man to be born, and according as he was like the Father he rose again; suffering wounds and saviour of the sick, one of the dead and giver of life to the dying, descending to the underworld and not departing from the Father's bosom. Hence also the soul which he laid down by the common condition, he soon took up again by his singular might and wonderful power. That these things are so and ought to admit no doubt, that is, that our Lord Jesus Christ should not be believed either not to be God amid the sufferings of his body, or to be God only, and not also man, amid the astounding works of his wonderful powers, he has taught us by setting before us the example of two apostles, declaring Christ our Lord to be God by the faith of Peter, and man by the doubt of Thomas. For what purpose was there in his wishing to ask his disciples whom men said he was, except that, when Peter answered: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, he might make known that this was not disclosed by flesh and blood but revealed by the inspiration of God the Father, and that through the testimony of the praised answer the faith of the truth might be laid open? What purpose was there that, when the Lord appeared after the resurrection, Thomas alone either was absent from the others or alone doubted, except that the world might believe what the doubting disciple had examined, so that, while he allowed himself to be touched by the hands of one, what he was might be recognised by the whole body of the faithful? The doubt, then, was not introduced to reprove the disciple, but the instruction of posterity was sought. Or does it aim at anything else, that the same Lord (Luke 24) joined Cleopas and another disciple when, on their way to Emmaus, they were talking about him? And although they had learned of the Lord's resurrection through the women who had first come to the tomb, yet, that through their doubt he might give firmness to believers in ages to come, beginning from Moses and all the prophets he explained and showed that it had been necessary for Christ to suffer and so to enter into his glory, and that in him there was both the human nature, through the passion, and the divine, through the glory. These things are conveyed by many examples of the holy Scriptures, and they are not told to your religious conscience, venerable emperor, as though unknown; for the faith itself, which you constantly affirm, renders you this gift: it plants in your senses both love for itself and pours in the knowledge by which it may be affirmed the more diligently. And yet it concerns the stewardship entrusted to me that I too should not keep silent about things known even among those who know them, so that, as the preaching of catholics follows on in turn through the changes of time, what is unceasingly affirmed may gradually be believed without end. I could have discussed more broadly, according to the definitions of the ancients, these matters that concern the godhead and manhood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the two natures united in him without confusion, if there had to be a dispute against those who dissent from them; but since both the synodal ordinances and the doctrines of blessed Pope Leo are in everyone's hands, I believed it more fitting to touch briefly on a few things than to unfold everything. Now, indeed, it is enough to recognise and to beware, so considering property and essence that it is known what we must attribute to the person and what to the substance. Those who shamefully do not know these things, or conceal them with crafty impiety, while they leave out what is proper to the Son in the Trinity, lay snares for the unity. But if what has been said above is held fixed with strong roots, there is no departing from the fathers' tradition, and questions are steadfastly met. DECREES OF POPE GREGORY THE YOUNGER.

In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, in the reign of our lord, the most pious Augustus Leo, crowned by God, great emperor, in the sixth year, the sixth year after his consulship, and also of Constantine his son, the new emperor, in the second year, in the month of April, in the fourth indiction.

The most holy and thrice most blessed Gregory, apostolic pope, presiding in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before the confession, with the most holy bishops also seated together:
Benedict, deacons, and all the clergy,

Gregory, the most holy and most blessed pope, said: Since by heavenly mercy we are rulers of the Lord's people, it befits us, with God's protection, to think the more zealously and often about their salvation, lest, if the souls entrusted to us are thwarted (God forbid) by the snares of the ancient enemy, we be compelled to render a strict account before the shepherd of all, unless correction of offences comes first by forestalling them. And while I weigh and call to mind with how much circumspection we ought, in keeping watch, to oppose the wickedness of each man's crime, and, if ever [the enemy] leaps in to disturb the minds of the faithful, to resist his blow with heavenly help, I am greatly shaken and waste away exceedingly, lest with serpentine cunning (God forbid) he deceive the more frivolous too. With God truly favouring [us], with great care of soul and a more even mind, relying on divine aid, we must strive for the salvation of all, so that with unabashed face, not struck down by anyone's fraud, we may be found worthy to stand before the eternal Judge and to hear the voice saying: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25; Luke 19). For hence it is that I say with groaning that I hear some of the Christian people dwelling throughout this province of Italy hold [practices] against the catholic faith and the statutes of the Fathers, so that they presume to take as wives women consecrated to God, and join their kinswomen to themselves in marriage; which ought to be cut off with the spiritual sword and, if it pleases your holiness, torn out by the roots, lest the crop of the good farmer, mixed with the bristling fruits of tares, be fouled (Matt. 13).
The most holy bishops and the venerable presbyters answered:

We truly recognise that the heart of your apostolate has been kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that the filth of such great wretchedness may be wiped from the minds of the faithful, and, as it were a wound fixed in the body, may be cured with a saving antidote once the entry of such wretchedness is barred; as has been well provided by the prohibition of anathema, so that no one again, whether Roman, Lombard, or of whatever nation, and washed in the water of holy baptism, may attempt this, lest, weighed down by the mass of so great a sin, he fall headlong or be plunged in the abyss of iniquity: it ought to be shunned and torn out by the roots.
After this unanimous response of all, Gregory the apostolic pope, before the body of the aforesaid venerable prince of the apostles of Christ, delivering sentence, said:
I. If anyone takes a presbytera in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
II. If anyone takes a deaconess in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
III. If anyone takes in marriage a nun, whom they call a handmaid of God, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
IV. If anyone takes his spiritual co-mother in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
V. If anyone takes his brother's wife in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
VI. If anyone takes his niece in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
VII. If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
VIII. If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
IX. If anyone takes as wife [a woman] of his own kindred, or one whom a kinsman had, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
X. If anyone steals a widow for a wife, or [anyone] consenting with him, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
XI. If anyone steals a virgin for a wife, unless he has betrothed her, or [anyone] consenting with him, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
XII. If anyone heeds soothsayers, haruspices or enchanters, or uses an amulet, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.

XIII. If anyone in any part violates the precepts previously issued by the apostolic Church concerning olive groves and various places, and does not observe them in all things, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.

XIV. To Hadrian son of Exhilaratus, who, after an oath sworn at the apostolic confession, with unlawful daring holds the deaconess Epiphania as wife: let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
XV. The deaconess Epiphania, who after an oath sworn slipped away in flight with Hadrian son of Exhilaratus to be his wife: let her be anathema; and all answered three times, Let her be anathema.
XVI. If anyone gives them assent in so cruel [a deed], let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
XVII. If anyone of the clergy lets his hair grow long, let him be anathema; and all answered three times, Let him be anathema.
